activities.anchor: survives because it is exactly right
activities.caption: pair each demonstration with what it proves
activities.name: perInferenceMatch

config.prompt: Identical input, different experience — pair each demonstration with what it proves:

pairs.right: identical 2-D pattern, two 3-D readings — the page sends one image, your experience flips
two different images, one per eye, alternating in awareness while both eyes keep reporting
a mouth saying 'ga' dubbed with audio 'ba' is heard as 'da' — lip reading fused with sound
the same ambiguous sound heard differently depending on the sentence around it — priors at work

config.why: The brain combines incoming evidence with prior expectations and reports the posterior — the most probable world. Identical input yielding different perceptions is the proof that construction is happening.

activities.anchor: Everything on this page, from the Necker cube
activities.caption: find the faulty line — a vision briefing
activities.name: perEyeSpot

config.prompt: One line of this vision briefing is wrong — click it:
lines: The retina delivers a sparse, two-dimensional, upside-down signal.
The signal has a hole — the blind spot — and veins crossing it.
What you experience is a reconstruction built from that signal plus expectations.
The eyes do the seeing; the brain merely receives the finished picture.
config.correction: The experience is constructed below consciousness — the Necker cube and the McGurk effect are that construction caught changing its mind about identical input.
config.why: Which is why an illusion is not a defect of the eye but an inference engine running its usual computation on engineered input.

activities.anchor: The 3-D world is rebuilt from cues
activities.caption: file each depth cue by its eye count
activities.name: perCueBuckets

config.prompt: Binocular or monocular? File each depth cue:
buckets: monocular — works in pictures and with one eye

items.label: retinal disparity — each eye gets a slightly different view
convergence — the eyes' angle for near objects
occlusion — nearer objects cut off farther ones
texture gradients — grain gets finer with distance
aerial haze and height in the plane
motion parallax — depth from your own movement

config.why: Given the cues, the brain maintains size constancy: perceived size is computed as image size × computed distance — and random-dot stereograms show depth can appear from patterns with no object contours at all.

activities.anchor: no amount of being told changes what you see
activities.caption: true or false — defects or engine
activities.name: perIllusionJudge

statements.s: Illusions are properties of a normally functioning inference engine fed tricky inputs.
statements.why: The machinery is doing its usual job on impossible inputs.

statements.s: Illusions are defects of the eye.
statements.why: The engine functions normally — the input is engineered to expose it.

statements.s: In Adelson's checker-shadow image, two squares with identical reflectance look black and white because the brain discounts the shadow.
statements.why: Lightness constancy at work — the cleanest demonstration of the point.

statements.s: Knowing the trick finally makes the two squares look identical.
statements.why: The computation runs below consciousness — knowledge does not reach it.

activities.caption: drag the divider — vase or faces
activities.name: perVaseCompare

config.prompt: Reversible figures: the same edges, two assignments — drag the divider.

before.label: the vase reading
before.text: The central region is the object; the two dark profiles recede into background.

after.label: the faces reading
after.text: The same edges now belong to two faces in profile; the vase is the gap between them.

config.why: Figure-ground segregation: every edge must be assigned to an object or its background, and reversible figures show the assignment flipping. The slogan is usually misquoted — the whole is other than the sum of the parts: grouping creates properties (a melody, a face) that exist at no single element.

activities.anchor: The eyes deliver far more than the mind processes
activities.caption: scrub the dated studies of the lesson
activities.name: perDatesTimeline

events.title: Cherry's dichotic listening
events.text: Participants shadow one ear's message and report almost nothing from the other — though their own name still breaks through.

events.title: Segall, Campbell and Herskovits
events.text: The Müller-Lyer illusion found far weaker in non-carpentered environments — 'universal' illusions can be learned statistics of a built world.

events.title: Pozzulo and Lindsay
events.text: Target-present and target-absent line-ups: children especially prone to false identification when the culprit is absent.

events.title: Simons and Chabris
events.text: About half of viewers counting passes fail to see a person in a gorilla suit stroll through the scene.

events.title: The revised Eyes Test
events.text: 36 photographs of the eye region, four mental-state words each — a perception study that doubles as a clinical instrument.

events.title: Andrade's doodlers and Henrich's WEIRD
events.text: Doodlers recall about 29% more; psychology's 'universal' laws audited as learned statistics of Western samples.

events.title: The dress
events.text: One photograph splits viewers into two constructed worlds — neither camp wrong about its own perception.

activities.anchor: turns the gate into a practical finding
activities.caption: call the doodling dividend
activities.name: perDoodleEstimate

config.prompt: In Andrade's doodling study, doodlers recalled roughly how much more than controls?
config.why: About 29% — roughly 7.5 of the 8 target names and places versus 5.8 for controls, and more of the 'go to the meeting' cues detected. The interpretation is attentional: doodling absorbs spare capacity without touching the verbal system — interference is channel-specific.
config.context: The right fidget can be better than forced stillness.

activities.caption: bet before you pick a camp
activities.name: perDressPredict

config.q: A photograph of a dress splits viewers almost exactly into two camps. According to this lesson, who is wrong?
choices: The blue-and-black camp — the illumination was obviously artificial
The white-and-gold camp — the image was plainly overexposed
Neither camp is wrong about its own perception — ambiguous illumination let different priors drive opposite constancy solutions
Both camps — the dress had no colour
config.why: Colour constancy works by discounting the illuminant: estimate the light source, correct the surface. The image's ambiguous illumination let daylight-versus-artificial priors, held with different strengths, drive opposite solutions — one image, two constructed worlds, the entire lesson compressed into a JPEG.
